transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-03-16
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~42 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Derek (Redwood SE), Priya (CSM); Lina (CTO), Samir (SRE), Rachel (PM), Jorge (DevOps)

Auto-generated summary (may be imperfect):
- Brief RCA review of yesterday's 15:17 spike; 502 cascade from overloaded inference nodes and concurrent requests steered to fallback model variant; backlog grew for ~3m, then circuit opened.
- Discussed client retry behavior: Samir's team uses exponential backoff but with high concurrency leading to retry storms.
- Agreed to run traffic replay and tighten retry budget + add jitter; Redwood to propose burst window config.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya: okay so uh hi everyone, thanks for joining the POC weekly. can we do quick roll call?
[00:06] Lina: yeah lina here. Samir?
[00:08] Samir: Samir on for SRE. Rachel here. Jorge as well.
[00:12] Derek: Derek from Redwood, hey all. Priya also on.
[00:15] Maya: great, agenda for 30 minutes is: quick incident followup, replay results, retry strategy, burst capacity options, and next steps. sound good?
[00:22] Lina: yep good. quick note, legal wants an update on private timing but we can cover later.
[00:27] Maya: ok cool. Samir, can you summarize the spike? I think you had some new logs.
[00:33] Samir: yeah so around 15:17 yesterday we saw qps jump from 120 to 520 over ~45s. that pushed several workers to queue; some requests hit 502s and our client retried a bunch which amplified it. um the weird part was that the KV cache hit rate dropped to like 22% during the surge which increased per-request latency.
[00:50] Rachel: just to add, user journeys that hit long sequences escalated cost too; a lot of these calls had 1.6k token contexts.
[00:58] Derek: ok that maps to what we saw server-side — small pool of workers became hot for a subset of keys, hotkeying on inference shard. the runtime started shedding load by returning 502s once queue depth passed our threshold.
[01:12] Jorge: is that threshold configurable? we don't want opaque circuit behavior.
[01:17] Derek: yes it's configurable per-model. right now you're on the default conservative setting; we can open the window for short bursts or add a graceful degrade to smaller model variant rather than immediate 502.
[01:28] Maya: quick interjection — two options we'd propose: short burst window (6-12s) with controlled queueing + adaptive fallback to half-size quantized variant. or tighten client retry budget with jitter so retries don't coincide.
[01:42] Samir: we already do exponential backoff but our client has high fanout — basically 50 workers per request layer — so even with backoff you get a lot of retries queued.
[01:54] Lina: and we have a hard SLA internally that client won't block longer than 2s, so increasing client patience is hard.
[02:02] Derek: understood. then server-side mitigations are more relevant: shorten cold-path latency with prefix caching, ensure KV cache warms up on replay, and introduce token-bucket style ingress limiter to smooth bursts.
[02:16] Rachel: can you explain prefix caching again? I thought KV cache was automatic.
[02:21] Derek: yeah so KV cache is automatic but prefixes help — if you have common starting tokens we can pre-populate KV cache entries during warmup or reuse partial state for repeated prompts; that reduces first token overhead. sometimes the tokenizer differences cause misses, so we'll look at normalizing prompts.
[02:38] Maya: quick note, transcription may mess up some product names — when Derek says KV cache he means the runtime K-V attention cache.
[02:44] [crosstalk] Jorge: ok — sorry, just trying to understand: if we enable a 10s burst window, what's the impact on cost?
[02:51] Maya: rough guesstimate: short bursts increase CPU/GPU duty for those seconds, maybe 8-14% unit cost increase depending on frequency; but reduces 502s and downstream retries which saves client-side compute, so net cost could be neutral or slightly positive. we'll run cost simulations.
[03:07] Samir: earlier you mentioned falling back to a smaller variant — does that change output quality?
[03:12] Derek: yes slightly. half-size quantized might have more tokenization quirks and occasional score drift on specialized medical terminology. we can gate fallback to only non-critical routes or add verification step.
[03:25] Rachel: for clinical triage flows we need high fidelity — can't fallback there.
[03:29] Maya: noted — we'll create route-level policies.
[03:33] [05:00] Derek: I ran an internal replay this morning with synthetic spikes; key findings: if KV cache warms to >65% hit before surge, tail lat decreases by ~220ms and 502s reduce by 70%. but if hit rate is <30% you see queueing and 5xxs climb.
[05:20] Samir: interesting — our observed 22% aligns. what's causing the low hit? cold starts or prompt variability?
[05:28] Derek: combination. long contexts plus per-request prompt variations and sometimes user-specific prefixes. also some clients send session tokens that vary and break caching.
[05:38] Lina: are there quick fixes we can do on our side? maybe normalize prompts server-side?
[05:43] Derek: yes normalizing templates and removing volatile metadata from prompts helps. also pre-warming common session prefixes during low-traffic windows works.
[05:52] Jorge: how invasive is pre-warm? do we need infra changes?
[05:56] Derek: not heavy — Redwood can trigger warmup requests via our API; we can provide a small runner script or you can call an endpoint.
[06:04] Rachel: can you share the runner?
[06:06] Maya: yes we'll include a sample warmup script in the follow-up.
[06:10] [08:00] Samir: about retries — what's the recommended client policy? our current retry budget is 5 attempts with backoff starting at 100ms, doubling.
[08:11] Derek: that's aggressive. recommend: cap total retry budget to 2-3 attempts, initial backoff 200-300ms, add full jitter, and use circuit-breaker that marks model unhealthy for N seconds after X 5xx per minute. also prefer idempotent vs non-idempotent differentiation.
[08:33] Lina: but that means some calls will fail; we want graceful degradation.
[08:37] Derek: combine reduced retries with fast fallback to a cheaper variant or cached response for non-critical queries. for critical queries maintain higher fidelity path.
[08:47] Maya: quick check — competitor question: have you evaluated Anthropic's approach to burst handling? Lina: we looked briefly, but they don't offer the same runtime observability you have, so we're leaning here.
[09:00] [10:30] Derek: regarding rate windows — we can set a sliding window burst allowance per tenant: e.g., allow 5x baseline for a 10s window but throttle down for the next 60s. that avoids long tail overloads.
[10:45] Samir: can we see a sim of 5x for 10s then drop? how does token accounting work?
[10:52] Derek: token accounting counts generated tokens per window; we'll provide a simulation spreadsheet. Maya: action: Derek will run a replay sim with your traffic and return histograms.
[11:03] Rachel: any changes required to our SDK?
[11:06] Derek: minimal — we'll send client guidance for retry/backoff and sample code to implement full jitter. also SDK option to prefer fallback model.
[11:16] [15:00] Samir: about the 502s — logs show a correlated pattern with GC pauses in the worker JVM (we run a small pre/post pipeline). could that be amplifying queueing?
[15:09] Derek: GC pauses can definitely add to request latency variance. if your pipeline adds 100-200ms occasionally, that pushes GC + inference over thresholds. consider moving pre/post processing async or off the hot path.
[15:24] Jorge: noted, we'll investigate moving preproc off the request thread.
[15:28] Lina: legal note — if we move to private deployment, does Redwood keep audit logs in our VPC?
[15:34] Maya: yes Private offers local control plane and we can integrate with your KMS and push logs to your s3. we'll send the compliance pack.
[15:42] Priya: I'll attach SOC2/ISO artifacts in the follow-up.
[15:46] [18:00] Derek: one more datapoint: replay with staged warmup, where we pre-warmed the top 200 session prefixes, reduced the 99.9th by ~1.1s in our test. it looked promising.
[18:15] Samir: ok that suggests a path: 1) normalize prompts, 2) implement warmup runner, 3) tighten retry budget + jitter, 4) enable short burst windows with fallback.
[18:29] Maya: agreed. does anyone object to that plan?
[18:33] Rachel: no objections. need to mark clinical routes as no-fallback though.
[18:38] Derek: we'll add route-level policies in the config.
[18:41] Lina: timeline? we want to see replay results asap.
[18:45] Derek: I'll run a replay tonight and share artifacts by Friday morning your time.
[18:51] Maya: Maya will send pricing and burst window options by tomorrow. Priya will send compliance docs. Samir you'll share traffic profile — please include seq length distribution.
[18:58] [22:00] Jorge: quick question: if we enable the burst window, will warmup increase memory usage?
[22:06] Derek: yes a bit — KV cache entries use memory, but we can size it and TTL aggressively; we can also evict less-used prefixes.
[22:18] Rachel: any recommended TTL?
[22:21] Derek: start with 30 mins for active prefixes, tune down if memory pressure.
[22:28] [30:00] Maya: ok final recap — action items and owners listed in the notes. next call same time next week unless we need a KV cache deep-dive sooner.
[30:12] Lina: thanks everyone.
[30:15] Maya: thanks, bye.
